messages.content: I want to develop a learned turbulence closure that captures bidirectional energy transfer and remains stable across unseen coarse-graining scales. What does that goal require?

The closure needs to represent energy transfer in both directions while keeping kinetic energy bounded. Its quantitative target is energy-spectrum error below 10% against filtered direct numerical simulations at two unseen filter widths. It also needs correct mean subgrid dissipation while reproducing intermittent backscatter.
What do you mean by energy transfer in both directions?

In this context, forward transfer moves energy from resolved motions toward unresolved motions, while backscatter moves energy in the reverse direction. A bidirectional closure must be able to represent both, rather than treating subgrid transfer as exclusively dissipative.
If the mean subgrid dissipation is correct, why call out backscatter separately?

A mean describes a net effect. It can be correct even if the closure misses reversals of energy transfer. Reproducing intermittent backscatter adds a distinct requirement: the closure must allow occasional reverse-transfer events without losing the correct mean subgrid dissipation.
So intermittent backscatter does not mean energy should flow backward on average?

Right. The stated goal asks for intermittent backscatter and correct mean subgrid dissipation together. Occasional reverse transfer should not be confused with a requirement that the average transfer reverse direction.
How does that fit with keeping kinetic energy bounded?

Backscatter can add energy to resolved motions, so the stability requirement matters alongside it. The goal is not to prohibit reverse transfer; it is to reproduce intermittent backscatter without allowing kinetic energy to become unbounded. Bounded kinetic energy, correct mean subgrid dissipation, and bidirectional transfer are simultaneous requirements.
Would a closure that only removes energy be a simpler way to satisfy stability?

It might avoid one source of energy growth, but that alone would not meet this goal. A closure restricted to forward transfer would not capture bidirectional energy transfer or reproduce intermittent backscatter. Stability cannot stand in for those requirements.
What exactly is the energy-spectrum target?

The target is below 10% energy-spectrum error against filtered direct numerical simulations at two unseen filter widths. Both the threshold and the fact that the two filter widths are unseen matter: the goal is not merely to match a spectrum at a width already encountered.
Does meeting the target at one of those widths count?
No. The requirement names two unseen filter widths, so a result below 10% at only one would not satisfy that stated target. The closure also has to meet the energy and transfer requirements.
Why describe the scales as unseen?

It emphasizes that the closure should remain effective when applied at coarse-graining scales it has not previously encountered. The two unseen filter widths make that part of the goal concrete for the energy-spectrum comparison, without asserting performance at every possible coarse-graining scale.
Are the two widths specified numerically?
No numerical widths or units are specified here. What is specified is their number—two—and that both are unseen filter widths used for the comparison with filtered direct numerical simulations.
Is the 10% threshold about kinetic energy rather than the spectrum?

It is specifically an energy-spectrum error threshold: below 10% against filtered direct numerical simulations at the two unseen filter widths. Bounded kinetic energy is a separate stability requirement, and no numerical kinetic-energy bound is stated.
Does the goal say how energy-spectrum error is calculated?

No particular error formula is given. The stated comparison and threshold should be preserved without assuming a specific norm, weighting, or range of the spectrum. Those details would need to be defined before the threshold could be assessed unambiguously.
Could a good spectrum comparison alone demonstrate that the closure works?

Not against the full goal. Spectrum error below 10% at both unseen filter widths addresses the stated spectral target, but it does not by itself establish bounded kinetic energy, correct mean subgrid dissipation, or intermittent backscatter.
And could bounded kinetic energy alone establish that the modeled transfer is right?

No. Bounded kinetic energy addresses stability, not whether the closure has the correct mean subgrid dissipation or represents intermittent reverse transfer. A stable closure could still miss the bidirectional behavior the goal calls for.
Is intermittent backscatter just another name for bidirectional transfer?

They are related but have different emphasis. Bidirectional transfer says the closure must represent both forward and reverse energy transfer. Intermittent backscatter says the reverse transfer should appear as occasional events, rather than being absent or treated as the constant direction of transfer.
What does 'learned' commit us to here?

It identifies this as a learned turbulence closure. The goal does not specify an architecture, training procedure, or particular way to impose stability. Those choices are not needed to state the required behavior and comparisons.
Should 'remains stable across unseen coarse-graining scales' be read as a claim that stability has already been shown?

No. This is a development goal, not a report of a completed result. It calls for stability across unseen coarse-graining scales, with bounded kinetic energy stated as a required property; it does not say that property has already been demonstrated.
Then give me the complete objective in one statement without weakening any part of it.

Develop a learned turbulence closure that captures bidirectional energy transfer and remains stable across unseen coarse-graining scales, achieving below 10% energy-spectrum error against filtered direct numerical simulations at two unseen filter widths while maintaining bounded kinetic energy and correct mean subgrid dissipation and reproducing intermittent backscatter.
What kind of closure should we train to pursue the goal?

A proposed approach is a log-filter-width-conditioned equivariant closure that combines mean-dissipation-calibrated eddy viscosity with energy-budget-capped stochastic backscatter. It separates a contribution intended to account for mean dissipation from one intended to represent intermittent reverse energy transfer, while limiting the latter through an energy-budget cap.
What is conditioned on the log filter width?

The learned closure is conditioned on the logarithm of the filter width, so its behavior can depend on the coarse-graining scale at which it is applied. The proposal does not specify a particular model architecture or how that conditioning is implemented.
Why include the filter width at all?

The goal includes performance across unseen coarse-graining scales. Making filter width an input gives the closure information about the scale at which it is operating. That is a proposed way to address scale dependence, not a guarantee that it will generalize to unseen widths.
Is the logarithm being taken of the energy spectrum?

No. 'Log-filter-width-conditioned' refers to conditioning on the logarithm of filter width. The energy spectrum is a separate quantity used in the goal's comparison against filtered direct numerical simulations.
What does equivariant mean in this proposal?

An equivariant closure is designed so that its output transforms consistently when its inputs undergo the transformations for which equivariance is imposed. The proposal calls for equivariance but does not name a particular transformation or prescribe how to build that property into the model.
How do the two transfer contributions differ?

The eddy-viscosity contribution is to be calibrated for mean dissipation. The stochastic backscatter contribution is intended to allow reverse energy transfer, with its contribution capped by an energy budget. Combining them is a way to pursue both the mean-dissipation and intermittent-backscatter requirements rather than asking one contribution to serve both roles alone.
Does mean-dissipation-calibrated mean every local transfer must be dissipative?

No. Calibration for mean dissipation concerns the mean, while the proposal also explicitly includes stochastic backscatter. The closure is meant to permit reverse-transfer events without giving up the requirement for correct mean subgrid dissipation.
And does stochastic backscatter mean the mean transfer must reverse?
No. Stochastic backscatter is the proposed means of representing reverse-transfer events. It does not change the separate requirement for correct mean subgrid dissipation.
Why cap the backscatter with an energy budget?

The cap is intended to limit the energy supplied by the backscatter contribution, since the closure must reproduce intermittent reverse transfer while maintaining bounded kinetic energy. The proposal names an energy-budget cap but does not specify its mathematical form or claim that it has already established stability.
Would the cap simply eliminate any backscatter event?

That would conflict with the proposal's purpose. It calls for stochastic backscatter that is capped, not for removing backscatter altogether. The intended distinction is between allowing reverse transfer and leaving its energy contribution unconstrained.
If the cap is present, can we assume kinetic energy will remain bounded?

No. An energy-budget cap is a proposed stability measure, not proof of bounded kinetic energy across unseen coarse-graining scales. Bounded kinetic energy remains a requirement to establish for the resulting closure.
Does conditioning on log filter width establish the spectrum target at unseen widths?

No. Conditioning is part of the proposed model, not an outcome. The stated target remains below 10% energy-spectrum error against filtered direct numerical simulations at two unseen filter widths; whether the trained closure meets it would still need to be determined.
Could the stochastic part help with backscatter but still leave the spectral error too high?

Yes. Representing backscatter and meeting an energy-spectrum error threshold are distinct requirements. The proposed components indicate how to pursue them, but their presence alone does not demonstrate below 10% error at either unseen filter width.
Could mean dissipation be correct even if the intermittent behavior is wrong?

Yes. A correct mean is not, by itself, evidence that intermittent backscatter is reproduced. That is why the proposal includes a separate stochastic backscatter contribution, and why both properties remain important when assessing the closure.
Is the eddy viscosity fixed, or is it part of what gets learned?

The proposal is to train a learned closure combining these contributions, but it does not specify which parameters belong to each contribution or whether any are fixed. It does specify that the eddy-viscosity contribution is calibrated for mean dissipation.
Have we specified how to calibrate mean dissipation or choose the energy budget?

No. The proposal identifies mean-dissipation calibration and an energy-budget cap as features of the closure, without giving a calibration procedure, a budget definition, or a numerical cap. Those details should not be treated as settled by this proposal.
So what is the relationship between this proposal and the broader objective?

It is a proposed decomposition of the closure needed for that objective: filter-width conditioning addresses variation in coarse-graining scale; equivariance constrains how the closure responds to relevant transformations; calibrated eddy viscosity addresses mean dissipation; and capped stochastic backscatter addresses reverse transfer while limiting its energy contribution. The combined closure would still need to satisfy the objective's spectrum, kinetic-energy, mean-dissipation, and intermittent-backscatter requirements.
State the training proposal concisely, without implying that its performance has been verified.

Train a log-filter-width-conditioned equivariant turbulence closure that combines mean-dissipation-calibrated eddy viscosity with energy-budget-capped stochastic backscatter. Its ability to meet the stated targets remains to be established.
How should the backscatter energy cap scale with filter width to preserve extreme transfer events without destabilizing coarse-grid integration?

There is no specified scaling law yet. The cap needs to leave room for extreme reverse-transfer events at each filter width while limiting the energy they can inject into the coarse-grid integration. Making it too restrictive could suppress the events the closure is meant to reproduce; making it too permissive could undermine bounded kinetic energy. Those competing requirements frame the choice, but they do not determine a formula.
Should the cap increase as the filter width increases?

That direction cannot be inferred from the proposal alone. Whether a larger filter width calls for a larger or smaller numerical cap depends in part on what quantity the cap limits and how that quantity is defined. The requirement is appropriate behavior across unseen coarse-graining scales, not a stated monotonic relationship between cap and width.
What distinction about the capped quantity matters?

A cap on an amount of energy is not automatically interchangeable with a cap on a rate of energy transfer. Their numerical values would have different meanings, so a width-scaling rule cannot be specified precisely without first knowing what the energy-budget cap actually limits. The proposal does not define that quantity or its mathematical form.
Could we just use the same numerical cap at every width?

A constant cap is not ruled out by the wording, but neither is it justified by it. Its effect on extreme events and kinetic-energy stability could differ between widths. The important question is whether the chosen cap preserves intermittent backscatter without allowing the integration to become unstable, including at unseen widths.
Would conditioning the closure on log filter width automatically make the cap scale correctly?

No. Log-filter-width conditioning tells us that the learned closure can depend on filter width. It does not specify whether the cap depends on width, how it would do so, or whether any resulting dependence would preserve extremes and stability.
Is the cap supposed to remove the largest backscatter events?

The question calls for preserving extreme transfer events, so eliminating them indiscriminately would work against that aim. At the same time, an energy-budget cap limits how much reverse transfer can contribute. The unresolved issue is how to place that limit so it does not erase the intermittent behavior being sought or permit destabilizing energy input.
Does preserving an extreme event mean it must be completely unaffected by the cap?

Not necessarily. Preserving extreme events means retaining meaningful intermittent reverse-transfer behavior; it does not, by itself, require every proposed event to pass through without any limit. The node does not specify how closely capped events must match their uncapped magnitudes.
If the mean subgrid dissipation is right, can the cap be considered adequate?

Not on that basis alone. Correct mean subgrid dissipation can coexist with a loss of intermittent backscatter, and it does not establish bounded kinetic energy. Adequacy of the cap has to be considered in relation to both the extreme-event behavior and coarse-grid stability.
And if kinetic energy remains bounded, could the cap still be too strict?

Yes. A cap could keep kinetic energy bounded yet suppress the reverse-transfer events the closure is meant to reproduce. Stability is necessary for the goal, but it is not a substitute for intermittent backscatter.
How does the energy-spectrum target enter this question?

It remains a separate requirement on the resulting closure: below 10% energy-spectrum error against filtered direct numerical simulations at two unseen filter widths. A proposed cap-scaling choice cannot be judged solely by whether it bounds kinetic energy or allows backscatter; it must not be assumed to meet that spectral target either.
Can equivariance tell us the width-scaling exponent?

No exponent is specified. Equivariance concerns consistent transformation of the closure's outputs under the transformations imposed on its inputs; by itself, that description does not supply a numerical law for the backscatter energy cap as filter width changes.
So is there a definite answer to 'how should it scale' at this point?

Not a definite numerical one. The question identifies a trade-off to resolve: a width-dependent cap, if used, must be permissive enough to preserve extreme intermittent transfer and restrictive enough to avoid destabilizing coarse-grid integration. No particular direction of change, exponent, threshold, or cap definition has been established.
What would an answer need to specify before we could interpret it?

It would need to say what energy-budget quantity is capped and how the cap varies with filter width. It would also need to make clear how that choice is assessed against extreme backscatter and bounded kinetic energy at unseen widths. Without those details, saying only that the cap 'scales with filter width' leaves the central question open.

I have a specific hypothesis for the cap: backscatter caps scaled as Δ²|S|³ will achieve at least 90% recall of DNS top-decile events while keeping kinetic energy within 20% of DNS at unseen filter widths. How should I read that claim?

It is a testable hypothesis, not an observed result. It proposes Δ²|S|³ as the scaling for the backscatter cap and sets two outcomes that must hold together at unseen widths: ≥90% recall of DNS top-decile events and kinetic energy within 20% of DNS. The first addresses preservation of extreme events; the second addresses excessive energy growth relative to DNS.
What roles do Δ and |S| play in the proposed scaling?

Δ is the filter width, and |S| is the magnitude appearing in the proposed scaling, conventionally associated with strain rate. The expression says the cap scales with the square of filter width and the cube of that magnitude. It does not, by itself, specify a proportionality coefficient or the complete cap formula.
Does the Δ² factor mean the cap is always larger at a coarser filter width?

If |S| and any other factors were held fixed, the Δ² factor would increase as filter width increases. Across actual coarse-graining scales, |S| need not remain fixed, so the full Δ²|S|³ factor need not increase in every comparison. The hypothesis specifies the scaling expression, not an unconditional ordering of cap values between widths.
And does |S|³ mean stronger local strain allows more backscatter?

For fixed Δ and other factors, a larger |S| gives a larger Δ²|S|³ factor. Interpreting that factor as setting the permitted backscatter contribution is consistent with the proposed cap, but the hypothesis does not give its exact implementation. In particular, it does not say that a larger cap necessarily produces a larger backscatter event.
Why pair top-decile recall with a kinetic-energy comparison?

They probe the two sides of the cap question. A stringent cap might suppress extreme transfer events, so the hypothesis asks for ≥90% recall of DNS top-decile events. A permissive cap might allow excessive energy input, so it also asks that kinetic energy stay within 20% of DNS at unseen widths. Satisfying only one would not satisfy the stated hypothesis.
Does ≥90% recall mean 90% of all backscatter events are reproduced?

No. The threshold is specifically recall of DNS top-decile events, not recall of all events. Recall concerns how many events in that DNS-defined extreme group are captured; it does not, on its own, describe the closure's behavior on the remaining events.
Is 'top decile' enough to know exactly which DNS events count?

It identifies a highest-ten-percent group, but the precise event definition and ranking criterion are not supplied. To evaluate the hypothesis, those choices would have to be made explicit. They should not be silently assumed from the phrase alone.
Could recall be high even if the closure also produces many extra extreme events?

Yes. Recall measures recovery of the selected DNS events; it does not, by itself, count extra events produced by the closure. The hypothesis states a recall threshold and a kinetic-energy comparison, but it does not state a separate threshold for extra extreme events.
What exactly does 'kinetic energy within 20% of DNS' tell us?

It states a relative comparison with DNS kinetic energy, with a 20% tolerance, at unseen widths. It does not specify which kinetic-energy statistic is compared or how comparisons across time are aggregated. It also should not be paraphrased as a claim that kinetic energy is always below DNS: 'within 20%' allows deviations on either side.
Does the 20% condition prove the coarse-grid integration cannot become unstable?

No. The condition is intended to constrain energy behavior relative to DNS, but the hypothesis does not supply a mathematical stability guarantee. Whether an integration remains stable must not be treated as established simply because the proposed comparison has a numerical threshold.
Is the claim that this scaling has already achieved both thresholds?
No. 'Achieve' here is what the hypothesis predicts. It has not been presented as a measured ≥90% recall result or as an observed kinetic-energy comparison within 20% of DNS.
Does this replace the goal of below 10% energy-spectrum error?

No. This hypothesis concerns the proposed backscatter cap, DNS top-decile event recall, and kinetic energy relative to DNS at unseen widths. The broader closure goal still includes below 10% energy-spectrum error against filtered direct numerical simulations at two unseen filter widths, as well as correct mean subgrid dissipation and intermittent backscatter. The hypothesis does not assert that those other requirements are met.
Could the cap meet its two predicted thresholds but the closure still miss the spectrum target?

Yes. Event recall and a kinetic-energy comparison do not automatically determine energy-spectrum error. Even if both predicted cap-related outcomes were observed, the spectrum target would remain a separate requirement.
Does scaling the cap as Δ²|S|³ determine the mean subgrid dissipation?

No. The proposed closure also includes eddy viscosity calibrated for mean dissipation. The cap hypothesis concerns the backscatter contribution and its relationship to extreme events and kinetic energy; it does not state that the scaling alone produces correct mean subgrid dissipation.
Should I say the hypothesis applies to exactly two unseen widths?

The hypothesis says 'at unseen widths' without specifying a number. The broader energy-spectrum goal explicitly names two unseen filter widths. It is best to keep those statements distinct rather than add an exact width count to the hypothesis.
Can you state the proposed claim in one sentence while preserving its uncertainty?

The hypothesis is that Δ²|S|³-scaled backscatter caps will achieve ≥90% recall of DNS top-decile events while keeping kinetic energy within 20% of DNS at unseen filter widths; neither outcome is asserted as established.
How should we compare a strain-scaled backscatter cap with a fixed cap?

The plan is to fit on isotropic DNS at filter widths Δ=8η and Δ=12η, then compare the strain-scaled and fixed caps at held-out widths Δ=10η and Δ=16η. The comparison focuses on backscatter recall and energy drift. This is a planned comparison, not a report of results.
Which widths are used for fitting, and which are held out?
Fit at Δ=8η and Δ=12η. Hold out Δ=10η and Δ=16η for the comparison. Here η is the scale in which the stated filter widths are expressed.
Why do both caps need to be compared at the held-out widths?

That places the strain-scaled and fixed caps under the same width conditions when comparing backscatter recall and energy drift. The plan asks how the cap choice behaves away from the fitting widths, rather than judging it only where fitting occurs.
Is Δ=10η really unseen if it lies between the fitting widths?
Yes. Held out means it is not one of the fitting widths. Numerically, 10η lies between 8η and 12η, but it is still a distinct filter width reserved for comparison.
And Δ=16η is larger than both fitting widths?

Yes. It exceeds both 8η and 12η. Thus the two held-out widths occupy different positions relative to the fitting widths: 10η is between them, while 16η is above both. That distinction does not predict how either cap will perform.
When you say 'strain-scaled,' are you specifying the exact cap formula?
Not in this plan. It names a strain-scaled cap as one side of the comparison but does not give its mathematical definition. The other side is a fixed cap; its numerical value is not specified either.
Does 'fixed' mean the backscatter contribution is constant?
No. The term describes the cap being compared, not necessarily the backscatter contribution itself. The plan does not say that every backscatter event has the same magnitude under the fixed cap.
What does backscatter recall measure in this comparison?

It concerns whether backscatter events are recovered. The plan names backscatter recall as a comparison measure, but does not specify an event definition, a recall threshold, or exactly how events are matched. Those details should not be read into the plan.
Does energy drift mean the same thing as bounded kinetic energy?

They are related concerns, but not identical statements. Energy drift is a measure the plan proposes comparing between the caps; bounded kinetic energy is a stability requirement for the closure. The plan does not define how drift is calculated or claim that any particular drift value establishes boundedness.
Should we expect the strain-scaled cap to have higher recall?

The plan does not state an expected winner. Comparing recall at Δ=10η and Δ=16η is how the two cap choices would be examined; neither higher recall nor lower energy drift is reported or guaranteed for either choice.
Could one cap have better recall but worse energy drift?

That is a possible outcome of a comparison with two measures, but not an outcome established here. Looking at both measures matters because preserving backscatter and limiting undesirable energy behavior are distinct concerns.
Are we fitting on isotropic DNS at all four widths and merely reporting two of them?
No. The stated plan fits on isotropic DNS at Δ=8η and Δ=12η. It reserves Δ=10η and Δ=16η as held-out widths for comparing the caps.
Does the plan say how many DNS cases or simulations are involved?
No. It identifies isotropic DNS and the fitting and held-out filter widths, but gives no count of simulations or further details about the data.
Are we comparing whole closures or just the cap choices?

The specified comparison is between strain-scaled and fixed caps, assessed through backscatter recall and energy drift at the held-out widths. The plan does not spell out how all other closure components are handled during that comparison.
Does this comparison by itself cover the energy-spectrum error target?

No. Backscatter recall and energy drift are the measures named in this plan. It does not specify an energy-spectrum-error comparison, so this planned cap comparison alone should not be described as demonstrating the broader spectrum target.
What about mean subgrid dissipation?

That remains part of the broader closure goal, but it is not named as a measure in this particular comparison. The plan specifically calls for comparing backscatter recall and energy drift; it does not report or prescribe a mean-dissipation result.
Can we already say that either cap works at unseen scales?
No. Δ=10η and Δ=16η are designated as held-out comparison widths, but no outcomes are supplied. The plan establishes where and on what measures to compare the caps, not what the comparison will find.
Please restate the plan without adding a predicted result or an unspecified metric definition.
Fit on isotropic DNS at Δ=8η and Δ=12η; then compare strain-scaled and fixed backscatter caps at held-out Δ=10η and Δ=16η using backscatter recall and energy drift.
What is the next activity for comparing the backscatter caps?

Run a posteriori large-eddy simulations (LES) at filter widths Δ=10η and Δ=16η, comparing a Δ²|S|³-scaled backscatter cap with a fixed cap. Measure top-decile backscatter recall and kinetic-energy drift for the comparison. This specifies an activity to carry out, not results from completed simulations.
What makes these simulations a posteriori?

In an a posteriori LES, the closure is used during the coarse-grid simulation, so its contributions interact with the evolving resolved flow. That makes kinetic-energy drift particularly relevant: the comparison examines energy behavior during integration, rather than only evaluating closure outputs independently of a running LES.
Which filter widths are involved in this activity?
The LES runs are at Δ=10η and Δ=16η. Both cap choices are to be compared at those widths; the activity does not report an outcome at either one.
Are we comparing two different filter widths or two different caps?

Both distinctions matter, but the cap comparison is the central one: Δ²|S|³-scaled versus fixed. The activity calls for that comparison at each of the two specified widths, 10η and 16η, so behavior can be examined at both widths rather than conflating a change of cap with a change of width.
What does Δ²|S|³ identify here?

It identifies the scaling of one backscatter cap: the square of filter width Δ times the cube of |S|, the magnitude in the strain-based scaling. The activity does not give a coefficient or a complete mathematical definition of the cap.
Does the fixed cap mean backscatter is switched off?
No. A fixed cap is the comparator to the Δ²|S|³-scaled cap; it is not a statement that backscatter is absent. Nor does the activity specify the fixed cap's numerical value.
Why measure recall in an actual LES rather than just look at the cap values?

The cap value alone does not tell us whether the running closure reproduces the extreme backscatter events of interest. Measuring top-decile backscatter recall in the a posteriori LES addresses that behavior directly. The activity does not yet say what recall the simulations will achieve.
What does 'top-decile backscatter recall' mean in this setting?

It is a measure of how many events in a designated highest-ten-percent group of reference backscatter events the LES captures. The associated hypothesis refers specifically to DNS top-decile events. This activity names the recall measure but does not spell out the event definition, ranking criterion, or matching procedure.
Would high recall tell us that the LES never produces spurious extreme events?
No. Recall concerns recovery of the selected reference events. It does not, on its own, measure extra events generated by the LES, and this activity does not specify a separate measure for them.
What is kinetic-energy drift meant to show?

It provides a way to compare the energy behavior of the two caps during coarse-grid integration. A backscatter cap is intended to allow reverse transfer without destabilizing that integration, so tracking kinetic-energy drift alongside recall addresses the other side of the trade-off. The activity does not define the drift calculation or supply a result.
If drift is small, can we say kinetic energy stays within 20% of DNS?

Not without a definition and the corresponding DNS comparison. The associated hypothesis predicts kinetic energy within 20% of DNS at unseen widths, whereas this activity explicitly says to measure kinetic-energy drift. Those are related energy questions, but the words alone do not make the drift measure identical to a within-20%-of-DNS test.
And is the ≥90% recall threshold part of what is measured here?

Top-decile backscatter recall is measured here. The associated hypothesis predicts ≥90% recall of DNS top-decile events, so the measurement can inform that prediction once the events and comparison are defined. The activity does not state that the threshold has been reached.
Should we expect the Δ²|S|³ cap to have both better recall and less drift than the fixed cap?

No result or ranking is given. The activity calls for comparing the two caps on both measures at 10η and 16η. It leaves open whether one cap performs better on either measure, or whether the measures point in different directions.
Could a cap preserve the top-decile events but still cause problematic energy behavior?

Conceptually, yes. Capturing extreme backscatter events and controlling energy behavior in an evolving LES are distinct aims. That is why this activity measures both top-decile recall and kinetic-energy drift instead of treating either as sufficient by itself.
Could low kinetic-energy drift compensate for missing most top-decile events?

Not for the stated purpose of preserving extreme transfer events. Low drift would address an energy-behavior concern, but poor top-decile recall would indicate a problem with the event-preservation side. The activity does not prescribe a way to trade one measure against the other.
Do these runs establish the below-10% energy-spectrum-error goal?

Not as specified. This activity names top-decile backscatter recall and kinetic-energy drift as its measurements. It does not include an energy-spectrum-error measurement, so the runs should not be described as establishing below 10% energy-spectrum error against filtered direct numerical simulations.
Does the activity state that mean subgrid dissipation is correct?

No. Correct mean subgrid dissipation remains part of the broader closure objective, but this activity does not report it or name it as one of the two measurements. Its specified measurements are top-decile backscatter recall and kinetic-energy drift.
Have the LES runs at 10η and 16η already been completed?

No completed runs or observed values are stated here. 'Run a posteriori LES' identifies the activity to perform; it should not be converted into a claim that the simulations have already produced results.
Restate the activity exactly enough to distinguish it from a prediction or result.

Run a posteriori LES at Δ=10η and Δ=16η, compare Δ²|S|³-scaled and fixed backscatter caps, and measure top-decile backscatter recall and kinetic-energy drift. The activity specifies what to compare and measure, not which cap will perform better or whether any predicted threshold will be met.
What did the a posteriori LES comparison show at 10η and 16η?

At Δ=10η, top-decile backscatter recall was 74% with the strain-scaled cap versus 69% with the fixed cap. At Δ=16η, it was 63% versus 57%, respectively. The reported kinetic-energy drift was below 12%. The strain-scaled cap had higher recall at both widths, but its recall missed 90% at both.
Can you pair each recall value with its width and cap again?
At 10η: 74% for the strain-scaled cap and 69% for the fixed cap. At 16η: 63% for the strain-scaled cap and 57% for the fixed cap. The strain-scaled cap is the Δ²|S|³-scaled choice in this comparison.
How much higher was strain-scaled recall than fixed-cap recall?

It was higher by 5 percentage points at 10η, from 69% to 74%, and by 6 percentage points at 16η, from 57% to 63%. Those differences describe the observed recall comparison; they do not explain what caused it.
Did the strain-scaled cap reach 90% recall at either width?
No. Its recall was 74% at 10η and 63% at 16η, both below 90%. It fell short of 90% by 16 and 27 percentage points, respectively.
What about the fixed cap—did it reach 90%?
No. Fixed-cap recall was 69% at 10η and 57% at 16η. The explicit comparison in the evidence is that the strain-scaled cap improved on those values while still missing 90%.
Does the result mean recall was the same across the two held-out widths?

No. Reported recall was lower at 16η than at 10η for each cap: 63% versus 74% for the strain-scaled cap, and 57% versus 69% for the fixed cap. The numbers show that difference; they do not establish its cause.
Does higher recall for the strain-scaled cap mean it reproduced all the extreme events?

No. Its 74% and 63% recall values indicate that it did not recover all the selected top-decile backscatter events. Higher recall than the fixed cap is a comparative finding, not complete event recovery.
How should I interpret the less-than-12% energy drift alongside the recall values?

The evidence reports energy drift below 12% despite recall remaining below 90%. In other words, the reported drift did not come with the targeted level of extreme-event recall. The statement does not define the drift calculation or break out a drift value for each cap and width, so those details cannot be inferred.
Can I assign the same drift percentage to all four cap-and-width cases?

No. There are four reported recall values, but only the aggregate statement that energy drift was below 12%. It does not give a separate drift percentage for the strain-scaled and fixed caps at 10η and 16η.
Does the evidence tell us which cap had less energy drift?

No. It supports a cap-by-cap comparison of recall, but it does not provide cap-specific drift values or a ranking on drift. The recall advantage should not be extended to an unreported drift advantage.
Is the less-than-12% drift a reason to describe the recall shortfall as unimportant?
No. The two measurements address different aspects of the comparison. The reported drift is below 12%, and the strain-scaled recall is below 90% at both widths. Neither observation erases the other.
